newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Gaddum - careful choice on EMU members needed.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Gaddum - careful choice on EMU members needed.

text.p: A senior Bundesbank official on Thursday said members of Europe's planned currency union, set to begin in 1999, must be chosen very carefully to ensure the new euro currency will be stable and strong.

Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, the Bundesbank's vice president, touched on the membership issue just days after Germany and Italy were engulfed in crisis as Italy insisted on joining EMU at the start and Germany allegedly argued for a delayed entry.

Despite a reassuring message from Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who said there were no differences between Germany and Italy on this point, German officials were said to be concerned about Italy's lack of fiscal consolidation and that its membership in the currency union could weaken the new currency.

Since European monetary and economic union is designed to bridge national differences, "the choice of participants at the start of (EMU) vitally important," Gaddum said in a speech prepared for delivery to the 32nd Conference of the Governors of South-East Asian Central Banks in Bangkok.
The selection process is all the more important as it is imperative the chosen group of nations is fairly "homogeneous with respect to their maturity for anti-inflation policy," Gaddum added.
His comments were released here ahead of the delivery time.
To join Europe's currency union, nations must show they have met certain criteria on budget deficits, government debt, inflation rates and exchange rates.
Countries' 1997 economic data will be reviewed in spring 1998, when a decision will be taken on which nations will quality.
Speaking at a time when German public opinion is turning lukewarm on the prospect of giving up the mark, Gaddum repeated that the currency union is designed as a "community of stability."
The future European central bank would be independent and the "statute of the European Central Bank defines ensuring price stability as its priority target," Gaddum added.

While the monetary union's fundamental position was clear, Gaddum said a number of other questions still needed to be cleared up, including choosing a target for monetary policy and whether the concept of minimum reserves will be adopted.

But Gaddum also said "the European Central Bank could demonstrate its responsibility more clearly and more transparently by means of the monetary targeting strategy" rather than using a direct inflation target."
He said "in future, a great deal will dependon the European Central Bank. Many people are pinning their hopes and expectations of a stable euro on its independence and steadfastness."
